title: Anatomy of an Infostealer
tagline: Follow a credential-stealer from first look to phone-home — and learn to read each move.

source.note: Illustrative, ATT&CK-accurate teaching example. NOT captured from executing a real sample. IPs use the RFC 5737 documentation range and example.com; nothing here is live.

stages.name: Surface — first look
stages.intro: Before running anything, an analyst reads the file's surface: its structure, strings, and imports. Here is what static triage shows.

events.detail: PE32 executable, .text section entropy 7.91/8.0 (very high — likely packed/compressed).
Embedded base64 blob (~40 KB) and the literal string "powershell -enc".

quiz.q: Which single observation most strongly suggests this file is packed?
options: It is a PE32 executable
The .text section has entropy of 7.91 out of 8.0
It imports VirtualAlloc
It contains the string "powershell"
quiz.explain: Near-maximum entropy (≈8.0) means the section's bytes look random — the signature of compression or encryption, i.e. packing. Imports and strings are hints about capability, but high entropy is the direct evidence of packing.

stages.name: Launch — it starts running
stages.intro: In a sandbox, the sample is executed. The first thing it does is spawn a hidden helper.

events.detail: PowerShell decodes the base64 command in memory and never writes it to disk.

quiz.q: Why launch PowerShell with -EncodedCommand and -WindowStyle Hidden?
options: To make the script run faster
To hide the real command from casual inspection and run without a visible window
Because PowerShell cannot run plain text
To improve compatibility with old Windows versions
quiz.explain: Base64-encoding hides the command from quick log inspection, and a hidden window avoids alerting the user. Neither is required to run PowerShell — both exist to stay quiet.

stages.name: Recon — is anyone watching?
stages.intro: Before doing damage, capable malware checks whether it is being analysed.

quiz.q: The sample looks for 'VBOX' and 'VMWARE' in device strings. What is it trying to decide?
options: Whether it has permission to run
Whether it is inside an analysis virtual machine
Which antivirus is installed
Whether the network is online
quiz.explain: Those strings appear on virtual disks/devices. Finding them suggests a VM — often an analyst's sandbox — so the malware may go dormant to avoid being studied. This is sandbox evasion (T1497).

stages.name: Persistence — surviving a reboot
stages.intro: To keep stealing after the machine restarts, the malware plants itself where Windows will re-launch it.

attck.name: Boot or Logon Autostart: Registry Run Keys

events.detail: Copies itself to %APPDATA%\svc\updater.exe and sets it hidden.

attck.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories

quiz.q: A new value appears under HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run. Which artifact is the persistence mechanism?
options: The %APPDATA%\svc folder
The Run registry key entry pointing at updater.exe
The hidden-file attribute
The base64 blob from earlier
quiz.explain: The Run key is what makes Windows re-launch the program at every logon — that is the persistence (T1547.001). The copied file and hidden attribute support it, but the Run entry is the mechanism itself.

stages.name: Exfiltration — the payoff
stages.intro: Now the real goal: collect secrets and send them out. Watch the network.

attck.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Web Browsers

events.detail: DNS query for cdn.example.com; TLS connection to 203.0.113.10:443.
HTTP POST of a 2.1 MB archive to https://cdn.example.com/upload — the stolen data leaving the host.

quiz.q: This is the moment your 外部流出 (exfiltration) logger fires. What just happened?
options: The malware downloaded an update
Stolen browser credentials were uploaded to an external server
The system checked for internet connectivity
A Windows service restarted
quiz.explain: It read the browser's credential store (T1555.003), then POSTed a 2.1 MB archive out to an external host (T1041). Data leaving the machine to an attacker-controlled server is exfiltration — the whole point of an infostealer.

recap.summary: You followed a full infostealer kill chain: a packed file that hid its real command, quietly checked for a sandbox, planted a Run key to survive reboots, then stole browser credentials and shipped them out. Each move maps to a MITRE ATT&CK technique — the shared vocabulary analysts use.

chain.name: Hidden PowerShell
chain.desc: Ran an encoded command in a hidden window.

chain.name: Sandbox evasion
chain.desc: Checked for VM and analysis tools.

chain.name: Credential theft
chain.desc: Stole browser logins and uploaded them.
